l: medical training, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie Inglis received medical training through hospital wards, dispensaries, operations, clinical observation, and examination preparation in Glasgow. Her training included surgery and was supported by teachers such as Dr. MacEwan.

l: surgery, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie Inglis could not take surgery in Edinburgh at the time, so she studied it in Glasgow. Dr. MacEwan allowed her to assist with an operation, and she worked to prepare herself for the surgical part of her qualification.

l: medical examination, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie Inglis prepared for the medical examination while studying and working in Glasgow. Despite worries about her memory and the questions she might face, she passed the examination with great success.

l: women's professional equality, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The unit presents women’s professional equality as a goal advanced through access to medical schools, mixed classes, university degrees, and professional training. The women students’ successful resistance to exclusion is described as part of a wider struggle for democratic rights in education.

l: Medical College for Women, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_intended_for women's medical education Elsie Inglis said that she wanted the first £20,000 she encountered to build and endow a woman’s college in Edinburgh. She regarded such a college as a possible response to the refusal to admit women to existing institutions.

l: Scottish medical profession, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The medical profession restricted women through limited clinical opportunities, inadequate laboratory access, and opposition to their full participation in medical education. Dr. Inglis fought these restrictions and sought equal opportunities for men and women in study, laboratory work, and professional practice.

l: Mrs. Scharlieb, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Mrs. Scharlieb, a woman doctor about forty, dark and solemn, was a visiting doctor at the New Hospital for Women. Particular but kind, she worked with Elsie on ward care and operations, advised her, discussed the hospital’s future as a qualifying institution, and expected Elsie’s future surgical consultation.

l: Mrs. Fawcett, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: leads Women’s Suffrage movement [as its acknowledged leader] CHAPTER VIII WAR AND THE SCOTTISH WOMEN ‘God the all-terrible King, Who ordainest Great winds Thy clarion, the lightnings Thy sword, Show forth Thy pity on high where Thou reignest, Give to us peace in our time, O Lord.] Millicent Fawcett led the National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies and supported the organisation of women for national service. She later recorded that the War Office’s refusal to recognise Elsie Maud Inglis was followed by grateful recognition from French and Serbian authorities.

l: New Hospital for Women, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The New Hospital for Women was a pioneering women’s hospital movement in Euston Road, London, founded for women patients and staffed by women doctors. By the time Elsie Inglis began working there, it had operated for nearly thirty years. It had four main wards, two small wards for serious cases, an extensive paying out-patient department with attractive waiting rooms, and women doctors including Garrett Anderson and Mrs. Scharlieb.

l: Dublin, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: contains the Rotunda Dublin is where Elsie stays at Costigan’s Hotel while training at the Rotunda from November 1893 into February 1894. During her stay she attends patients, encounters Irish political and religious divisions, and considers further study in Paris before returning to Edinburgh.

l: the First World War, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The First World War is an international conflict and the setting for invasion, epidemic, retreat, bombardment, shortages, hospital evacuations, and dangers at sea. As the approaching storm arrives, it tests nations and people’s hearts, suspends acute political disputes, and redirects women’s organisations toward national service. Mobilisation creates urgent need for medical care for the wounded and sends Dr. Elsie Inglis and her unit to battle fronts to aid nations allied in arms. The war brings deserted villages, refugees, destroyed stations, burning fuel tanks and grain ricks, disrupted schooling, and severe hospital conditions, alongside the typhus epidemic and the retreat involving Serbia and the Serbian Army. It also creates opportunities for women to replace men in wartime work and helps open a new era of women’s emancipation. Its hazards continue through the unit’s return voyage, with North Sea and other wartime maritime dangers. While the war is still ongoing, Elsie Inglis is honored at her funeral as a Red Cross worker who served abroad, with military honors, Allied flags, and representatives of the nations connected with her work.

l: women doctors, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Women doctors emerge as capable but contested medical practitioners. Though qualified and active in hospital work, they face exclusion from medical societies, college fellowships, and clinical opportunities often given to men, alongside assumptions that women cannot be doctors. Their work demonstrates demand: the New Hospital for Women records more than 20,000 outpatient visits in the year to November, while figures such as Miss D. and Miss MacGregor show professional achievement. At the Hospice, medical women gain opportunities denied in other maternity hospitals, as Dr. Inglis supports their education, clinical practice, laboratory access, and professional recognition.

l: patients, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: receive sunshine treatment [as a proposed treatment for recovery and health] Patients at the hospital included women whose illnesses had previously been dismissed as hysteria and others who had been given alarming or mistaken diagnoses. Elsie observed that patients with courage and stable nerves often recovered more quickly, and she described the hospital’s efforts to provide treatment, sunshine, and careful postoperative care.

l: medical practice, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Medical practice is portrayed as a demanding, compassionate vocation spanning hospital and private work. In London and Dublin during 1892–1894, it included ward rounds, temperature monitoring, cautery, anaesthesia, operations, outpatient care, consultations, and disputes over diagnosis and observation. Dr. Inglis later practised in Edinburgh with Dr. Jessie MacGregor, moving from Atholl Place to 8 Walker Street and earning a substantial income before combining practice with suffrage work and the Hospice. Elsie’s work served both paying and very poor patients, relying on kindness, sympathy, prescriptions, and disciplined acceptance of professional anxiety.

l: operations, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: are_performed_at New Hospital for Women [by women doctors with hospital anaesthetic support] Operations were a regular part of life at the New Hospital for Women, and Elsie assisted with several major cases. Some proceeded successfully, while one patient died after apparently doing well because she lacked the vitality to withstand the shock.

l: women’s hospital movement, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The New Hospital for Women represented the principle that women could practise the healing art and formed part of the wider women’s hospital movement. Its history was associated with Elizabeth Blackwell, Sophia Jex Blake, Garrett Anderson, and the growing professional work of women doctors.

l: hospital (the one being visited), Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a hospital The speaker uses this hospital as the model for the hospital they intend to build for themselves.

l: hospital for myself, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: A planned hospital for myself, intended if I do not get into the Infirmary in Edinburgh. It is to be built at the Cattle Market, at the head of Lady Lawson Street, comparatively high and convenient for women in Fountainbridge, the Grassmarket, and Cowgate; Eva’s hall is initially rented as a dispensary.

l: the Rotunda, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Rotunda in Dublin provides midwifery training through mixed classes, including clinical experience. It awards a Licentiate of Midwifery after six months and examination; Elsie takes three months’ training, praising its methods while noting women receive fewer clinical opportunities than male senior students.

l: the Home Rule question, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Home Rule question occupied Elsie Inglis’s political attention during the 1890s. She supported Home Rule, criticised obstruction and Lord Salisbury’s encouragement of resistance, and considered possible arrangements combining Irish self-government with Imperial Federation.

l: Dr. Jessie MacGregor, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Dr. Jessie MacGregor, a woman doctor and splendid pathologist, proposes that she and Elsie Inglis begin medical practice together in Edinburgh; Elsie believes their combined work could benefit both.

l: midwifery, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie’s training in midwifery at the Rotunda gives her confidence and extensive practical experience in the field. She feels that the Rotunda’s methods have prepared her to do important work in this branch of medicine.

l: the three-month Rotunda course, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a midwifery course [three months long] The three-month Rotunda course teaches Elsie a great deal about midwifery and makes her feel established in the subject. After three months she is told that she has learned all the Rotunda can teach her; she considers spending another three months studying in Paris instead of remaining for the six-month examination and Licentiate of Midwifery.

l: the proposed Edinburgh practice, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: A proposed Edinburgh medical practice for women doctors: Elsie and Miss MacGregor consider working together, starting a dispensary, then developing a Rotunda-like hospital with resident female students.

l: John Inglis’s death, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a death [borne with quiet patience] John Inglis dies on March 13, 1894, shortly after Elsie returns from Dublin. Elsie describes his quiet patience and says that she cannot imagine life without him, especially because they had made plans for her medical work that he had hoped to see begin.

l: death and the afterlife, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_described_as continued growth and learning [through all eternity] Death and the afterlife are presented as a passage into fuller life rather than simple ending. Dr. Inglis spoke of starting a new job on the other side, and those present felt triumph, peace, and a glorious presence after she died.

l: the Liberal Party, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: supports women’s justice [in stated principle but not the vote] Dr. Inglis was connected with the Liberal Party through the Central Edinburgh Women’s Liberal Association and the Women’s Liberal League. She severed her connection with the party when she became convinced that she could advance the cause of women more effectively without attachment to a party organisation.

l: Reni, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Reni is a small village beside the Danube, surrounded by Steppe, with shipping, a crowded wharf, and an important junction. By January 1917, the unit established a difficult-to-heat hospital there for badly wounded Russian Army and Navy patients connected with the evacuation station. Severe snow, mud, fuel shortages, and the frozen Danube affected its work. The Scottish Women’s Hospital base remained at Reni until it closed in August 1917.

l: Russia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Russia is a war-torn place and the route, field of service, and eventual danger zone for Dr. Inglis, Elsie, and a Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit serving alongside the Serbian army. Before the unit arrived to assist the Jugoslav Division, also described as the Serbian Division in Southern Russia, that force depended on Russian equipment and medical help. The unit traveled through Archangel and Moscow toward Odessa, receiving trains, food, repairs, transport, and other aid from Russian officials and civilians. Elsie traveled toward Russia, sought a copy of the Euchologion there, and worked under retreat conditions demanding rest and self-command. Russia is also a major war area marked by the Serbian Division’s battle, retreats, bombardments, disease, and uncertainty. Its people are portrayed as religious, interested in England, and hopeful after the war, but the Russian Revolution and a wider upheaval changed soldiers’ attitudes and made political and military conditions unstable. As the service ended, Inglis sought removal of the Serbian Army from the Russian front, while the Foreign Office feared for the unit’s safety amid the chaotic sufferings of the Russian people and evacuation.

l: Ireland, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Ireland was the subject of the Home Rule controversy discussed by Elsie Inglis and her father. Elsie supported giving Ireland control over its own affairs while preserving the unity of the Empire, and she argued that Irish members should remain in Parliament.

l: the Representation of the People’s Bill, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: recognises political enfranchisement [as its culmination] The Representation of the People’s Bill is presented as the measure that marked the victory of the common cause for which Elsie Inglis and her comrades had worked: women’s political enfranchisement.

l: the Home Rule Bill of 1893, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: provides Irish self-government [through its proposed constitutional framework] Elsie Inglis regarded the groundwork of the Home Rule Bill of 1893 as sound, though she believed it could be improved in committee. She supported retaining Irish members in Parliament and considered the proposed transfer of powers over police and land workable over time.

l: political enfranchisement, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Political enfranchisement is the common cause won by the generation’s suffrage movement, centered on ending women’s exclusion on the basis of sex through the Representation of the People’s Bill. Initially widely treated as a crank cause, it became a major question of democratic citizenship and national politics after the 1906 Liberal victory and elections. Organised pressure on Parliament sought women’s free rights of citizenship. Dr. Inglis placed enfranchisement above party organisation and left the Liberal Party when independent action better served women’s wider political freedom. During the war, women’s emancipation was connected to women replacing men who were fighting and dying; this challenged their treatment as irresponsible and was presented as opening a new era for women.

l: the British Parliament, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a national legislature [in which women first claimed citizenship] Parliament had long treated women’s franchise as an academic or marginal issue, with private members’ Bills often being talked out or talked round. After 1906, the question became a major unresolved political issue that placed pressure on successive Governments.

l: St. Giles’, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: St. Giles’ is a church central to Elsie Inglis’s healing mission, where she attended daily service and shared sympathy with friends after worship. It also became the site of Dr. Inglis’s final procession, funeral service, and burial, ending with the Hallelujah Chorus as the procession left.

l: militant suffragism, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: uses law-breaking [in pursuit of women’s enfranchisement] Militant suffragism emerged alongside the strengthened suffrage campaign and gave the press extensive publicity. Dr. Elsie Inglis deplored its law-breaking and believed that claiming a right to do wrong for a good purpose was closely related to anarchy.

l: Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Scottish Federation of Suffrage Societies was a federation carefully organised to coordinate Scottish suffrage societies and pressure Parliament. With Dr. Elsie Inglis as Honorary Secretary, it was strongly influenced by her policy from 1906 to 1914. In October 1914 it formally adopted the hospital scheme, chose the name Scottish Women’s Hospitals, and redirected suffrage organisations’ resources to wartime medical service as its final organisational scheme.

l: Suffrage societies, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: provide organisation and workers [for Scottish Women’s Hospitals] Scottish suffrage societies provided organisation and workers for the establishment of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. They supported Dr. Elsie Inglis’s work and its ideals even when the wider community wished to separate the hospitals from the unpopular suffrage cause.

l: the Scottish women, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Scottish women were politically organised through Women’s Suffrage societies and provided national service through voluntary work. During the war, they organised medical and practical service through the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, serving abroad as doctors, nurses, ambulance workers, and hospital staff.

l: women as citizens or as doctors, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: seek equal citizenship [through enfranchisement] Women are presented as seeking full citizenship, participation in public administration, and a greater role in the Church and State. The unit argues that women’s organised work had already made substantial contributions, despite continuing institutional prejudice against them.

l: the Vote, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a weapon for women’s citizenship [in the building of the New Jerusalem] The Vote was the central political objective repeatedly invoked by Dr. Elsie Inglis and her colleagues. She greeted supporters with hopes for a good year and the Vote, and described it as the weapon women could use to help build the New Jerusalem.

l: the Suffrage movement’s organisation, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Suffrage movement’s organisation was a federated political movement across social, professional, and industrial spheres, coordinated to pressure Parliament. It expanded through societies, workers, fundraising, meetings, debates, and a press campaign; Dr. Elsie Inglis’s administration and opportunism were important. Before the war it built efficient committees, organisers, speakers, and political networks, then redirected them from suffrage campaigning to national service and hospital units.

l: women’s medical service in wartime, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Women’s medical service in wartime developed despite official assumptions that women could not fight and were therefore not useful. Women doctors, nurses, ambulance workers, and orderlies organised professional service through the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. Dr. Elsie Inglis brought its units and equipment into existence, supported by Scottish suffrage societies. The service earned praise from allied nations.

l: University of Edinburgh, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The University of Edinburgh, an educational institution, first admitted women to examinations for medical degrees, where Dr. Inglis graduated M.B., C.M. in 1899. After previously refusing women medical students and certain extra-mural mixed classes, it opened its doors to women medical students in 1916 under a new head.

l: Central Edinburgh Women’s Liberal Association, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Dr. Inglis joined the Central Edinburgh Women’s Liberal Association in its early organised years and served as its Vice-President for sixteen years. She was one of its most active members, valued as a speaker and adviser, and respected for her enthusiasm for women’s welfare and her clear political judgment.

l: Muir Hall of Residence for Women Students, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Muir Hall of Residence for Women Students was founded in George Square to provide suitable accommodation for women students coming to the University from the country. Dr. Inglis served as honorary secretary until her death, helped students with illness and personal difficulties, and worked for their comfort.

l: Miss Mair, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: describes Elsie Maud Inglis [as courageous and decisive] CHAPTER VIII WAR AND THE SCOTTISH WOMEN ‘God the all-terrible King, Who ordainest Great winds Thy clarion, the lightnings Thy sword, Show forth Thy pity on high where Thou reignest, Give to us peace in our time, O Lord.] Miss Mair described Elsie Maud Inglis’s belief that women capable of surgery and medical diagnosis should be allowed to serve the sick and wounded. She also recalled the early decision to direct the energies of the suffrage societies toward starting a hospital.

l: Dr. Wallace Williamson, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Dr. Wallace Williamson, with his wife, shared vital discussions with Elsie after church and became an important friend. His teaching and friendship later helped her find the vital faith that inspired her life and work.

l: Maternity Hospice nursing and infant-welfare work, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Maternity Hospice nursing and infant-welfare work grew from a nursing home for working women into a maternity and infant-welfare centre serving a poorer district. Dr. Inglis promoted home visits, nurse training, infant care, a milk depot, health centres, and care designed around patients’ comfort and local needs.

l: district nursing, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: District nursing formed an important part of the Hospice’s service, with trained nurses visiting people in their own homes. By 1910 the number of cases exceeded the nurses’ capacity to attend them.

l: War Office, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: At the beginning of the war, the War Office rejects women’s offers of military medical service, including Elsie Maud Inglis’s expertise, and rejects Cargilfield as an auxiliary hospital. It operates military hospitals for military medical care; its position on women may change before the war ends.

l: surgical skill, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Dr. Inglis developed marked surgical skill while working in the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, where the pressure of work often kept her operating for days. This experience indicated that she might have become a great surgeon if she had received equal opportunities during her peace practice.

l: Elsie Inglis's family and friends, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie’s sisters lived near her in Edinburgh, and after her brother Ernest died in India in 1910, his widow and three daughters returned to her household. Her nieces remembered her thoughtful gifts, companionship, affection, and willingness to support their education, while friends and relatives shared holidays, Sunday suppers, conversation, bathing, golfing, and picnics with her.

l: the Church of Scotland, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie explored several Christian traditions before settling after her father’s death in the ministry of the Church of Scotland. Through its teaching and fellowship, especially that associated with Dr. Wallace Williamson, she found the faith that sustained her life and work.

l: retreats in Serbia or Russia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Those who accompanied Elsie on retreats in Serbia or Russia observed her strong self-command. When transport failed, she used the interval for rest rather than allowing circumstances to overcome her.

l: women's medical and civic service, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie’s increasing care over her dress was presented as adornment for the cause of women as citizens or doctors rather than for personal display. Her medical work and public service embodied that cause, and she welcomed the uniform associated with her work.

l: R. W. Seton-Watson, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: R. W. Seton-Watson, a historian and political writer knowledgeable about Serbia, supported Scottish Women’s Hospitals through the Servian Unit and praised Elsie Inglis’s heroic work in Serbia and on the Eastern front as a model of sympathy between nations.

l: National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies adopted the Scottish Women’s Hospitals plan on 15 October 1914. Through its London Branch, it helped raise money for new units, supported Elsie Maud Inglis’s mission to Serbia, and organized a Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit for the Serbian Army.

l: Serbian army, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Serbian army is an army closely linked to the Scottish Women’s Hospitals and Dr. Elsie Inglis. It had defeated its enemy in 1914 and was regarded by the Serbs as uniquely successful among the Great Powers’ forces. In 1915, facing Austrians, Germans, Magyars, and Bulgarians at about four times its numbers, it shortened its defensive line but could not resist German guns and the combined invasion. During the retreat, 160,000 soldiers escaped, while hospitals filled with wounded and streams of soldiers, stragglers, and refugees moved on. The Scottish Women’s Hospitals served the army with a fully equipped unit, treating wounded during the retreat; Inglis chose to return with the Serbian Army rather than leave it. On the Rumanian Russian front, Serbian wounded were evacuated to Odessa, and Russian officials and officers praised the soldiers’ courage and endurance. Soldiers in the Division were described as magnificent, disciplined fighting men able to stiffen Russian troops, while hospital orderlies were quick, devoted sanitaries. Later fighting after the Rumanians broke caused severe losses: 11,000 men from a division of 15,000. Serbian representatives travelled with Inglis and her unit and were to be brought away from the Russian front.

l: the Allied nations, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Allied nations are a coalition expected to aid Serbia during war and to receive medical assistance from the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, whose units served their armies and wounded. They matter chiefly because their failure to prevent Bulgarian mobilisation, stop the attack on Serbia from north and east, prevent the German breakthrough toward the Turks, or provide timely relief leaves Serbia exposed. Despite this, the Scottish unit hopes Allied action, including British troops at Salonika, may eventually help.

l: Serbian nation, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Serbian nation suffered epidemic, famine, crowded hospitals, and devastation by typhus after the Austrians invaded. Scottish women, including Elsie Maud Inglis, went directly to aid it. In gratitude, Serbians called Inglis “the angel of their people,” dedicated a simple fountain in Mladenovatz to her memory, and sent the Serbian Legation to her funeral, where representatives carried her coffin and lowered it into the grave.

l: World War I, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: World War I, beginning in 1914, is an armed conflict involving the Allied armies, the Serbian army, and fighting against a common foe, including near the Serbian and Romanian fronts. It created the circumstances for Elsie Maud Inglis and the Scottish Women’s Hospitals to provide foreign medical service in France, Serbia, and Russia, demonstrating women’s work in hospitals, camps, and support for armies and populations. As fighting intensified, the Serbian 1st Division faced a major battle against General Mackensen; retreats, movements of refugees and soldiers, bombardment, air raids, shortages, and overcrowded hospitals placed severe pressure on medical services. The conflict shaped Russia, Serbia, and other European nations and forms the setting for service during 1915 and Inglis’s death in 1917.

l: mobilisation, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: activates 6th Edinburgh V.A.D. [at the commencement of the war] CHAPTER VIII WAR AND THE SCOTTISH WOMEN ‘God the all-terrible King, Who ordainest Great winds Thy clarion, the lightnings Thy sword, Show forth Thy pity on high where Thou reignest, Give to us peace in our time, O Lord.] Mobilisation organised the armed forces but did not initially mobilise women’s strength in the same way. Elsie Maud Inglis’s 6th Edinburgh V.A.D. was mobilised at the beginning of the war, and she trained its members for service.

l: the truce, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: suspends women’s suffrage [as part of a general political truce] CHAPTER VIII WAR AND THE SCOTTISH WOMEN ‘God the all-terrible King, Who ordainest Great winds Thy clarion, the lightnings Thy sword, Show forth Thy pity on high where Thou reignest, Give to us peace in our time, O Lord.] The truce suspended questions of acute political difference, including the suffrage struggle. Although it was accepted by the whole people, the text says that it did not alter the commitment of the suffrage parties to their cause.

l: national service, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_provided_by the Scottish women [in response to wartime need] CHAPTER VIII WAR AND THE SCOTTISH WOMEN ‘God the all-terrible King, Who ordainest Great winds Thy clarion, the lightnings Thy sword, Show forth Thy pity on high where Thou reignest, Give to us peace in our time, O Lord.] National service gave the suffrage organisations a new wartime purpose after political campaigning was suspended. Elsie Maud Inglis and other women offered medical, nursing, organisational, and practical skills for service to the country and the Allied nations.

l: medical care for the wounded, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_provided_by Scottish Women’s Hospitals [for armies of the Allied nations] CHAPTER VIII WAR AND THE SCOTTISH WOMEN ‘God the all-terrible King, Who ordainest Great winds Thy clarion, the lightnings Thy sword, Show forth Thy pity on high where Thou reignest, Give to us peace in our time, O Lord.] Medical care for the wounded became a central concern after mobilisation and the formation of large military camps. Elsie Maud Inglis felt a strong personal responsibility toward wounded men and organised women doctors and nurses to provide care.

l: the Scottish Women’s Hospitals scheme, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: raises over £200,000 [for hospital work] CHAPTER VIII WAR AND THE SCOTTISH WOMEN ‘God the all-terrible King, Who ordainest Great winds Thy clarion, the lightnings Thy sword, Show forth Thy pity on high where Thou reignest, Give to us peace in our time, O Lord.] The Scottish Women’s Hospitals scheme developed rapidly in October 1914 from a proposal to establish a hospital into a larger organisation for foreign service. It aimed to send carefully selected, well-equipped, economical, and efficient units wherever they were needed.

l: the Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit for the Serbian Army, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit for the Serbian Army was a medical, hospital, nursing, and transport unit serving Serbian wounded and volunteers in wartime. In Serbia, the First Serbian Unit, led by Dr. Eleanor Soltau, worked during the typhus epidemic in crowded hospitals treating dying patients. At Kragujevatz, it nursed 550 beds across three hospitals: Reserve No. 3, a surgical hospital with an X-ray room and operating theatre; No. 6 Reserve, for typhus; and No. 7 Reserve, for relapsing fever and general diseases. As fever declined, it reorganised as tent hospitals near the front and prepared a disinfecting centre at Mladanovatz. During the Austro-German invasion and the 1915 retreat, 115 personnel remained with Serbian wounded. Under occupation at the Serbian military hospital at Krushieevatz, they treated extreme numbers of patients and fought typhus through sanitation, laundry, and bathing before being sent north under guard in February 1916. In 1917, an eighty-woman hospital and transport section travelled through Russia via Archangel and Moscow with fourteen cars to serve Serbian Volunteers on the Rumanian Russian front. Led by Dr. Elsie Inglis, it worked through evacuations, safeguarded its equipment, travelled west with Serbian soldiers, and cared for her during her final illness.

l: the Red Cross, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: CHAPTER VIII WAR AND THE SCOTTISH WOMEN ‘God the all-terrible King, Who ordainest Great winds Thy clarion, the lightnings Thy sword, Show forth Thy pity on high where Thou reignest, Give to us peace in our time, O Lord.] The Red Cross was involved in the development and recognition of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. The Scottish Red Cross’s head, Sir George Beatson, warned that the War Office would not support the women but acknowledged that its position might change.

l: Royaumont Abbey, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Royaumont Abbey, a large historic religious building in woods, became the Scottish Women’s Hospital site, whose staff extensively converted its architecturally significant spaces into a functioning hospital.

l: French Red Cross, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The French Red Cross supervised the hospital established by the Scottish Women’s Hospitals at Royaumont. An official of the French Red Cross was to live at the abbey with the hospital staff, and the unit awaited inspection by a French general.

l: Jugoslav Division, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Jugoslav Division was a military division of volunteers, Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes from Austria-Hungary, who had been taken prisoner by Russia and volunteered to fight for the Entente and Serbia, seeking Southern Slav unity under the national dynasty of Kara George. In the 1916 Dobrudja campaign, its main body fell from 15,000 to 4,000 and needed medical and equipment support. Commanded by General Haditch, its Serbian troops fought General Mackensen at a front called a second Verdun and were praised as heroes. After the Reni hospital closed, it received Scottish Women's Hospitals support and later prepared another move at Hadji Abdul.

l: Southern Slav unity, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Southern Slav unity was the national ideal that inspired the Jugoslav volunteers and attracted Inglis’s enthusiastic support. She regarded nationality as a foundation for a new and saner internationalism.

l: Joan of Arc, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Joan of Arc appeared to Inglis in an experience at Notre Dame, where a statue seemed to her to be alive. Inglis later wondered what Joan had been trying to say to her, and a ward at Royaumont was named after Joan of Arc.

l: Scottish Women's Hospitals unit at Royaumont, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: operates_under French Red Cross [at Royaumont] The Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit at Royaumont prepared the abbey for service despite having no fires, hot water, furniture, blankets, or complete equipment when it arrived. Its members scrubbed the building, assembled beds, and installed necessary facilities, while Inglis expressed pride in their practical and persistent work.

l: the Eastern front, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Eastern front is the setting of Inglis’s greater achievement after Serbia. It receives the Scottish Women’s Hospitals medical mission to help the Jugoslav Division through campaigns and privations; its hospital is praised by Russian soldiers, while Serbian troops are sought to strengthen Russian forces.

l: Dobrudja, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Dobrudja is identified as the place where the Rumanian and Russian refugees who will never forget "the angel of their people" were located.

l: Odessa, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Odessa is a port city with major shipping and wharf facilities. It hosts the British medical unit as guests and is the destination of its journey through Russia. Near Odessa, Elsie writes from an ambulance train in January 1917. The city then gives the unit an enthusiastic reception, providing officials, transport, quarters, and public celebrations, and shows deep interest in it. Elsie later returns to investigate absent Serbian patients. From Odessa, Inglis writes while Reni work closes and the unit prepares to join the Serbian Division; her last June 1917 letter praises that division.

l: Rumania, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Rumania was the location of the Serbian Army’s retreat and of major Scottish Women’s Hospitals work. At Galatz, Rumania, Dr. Inglis, her doctors, and nurses treated masses of wounded and performed operations and dressings for fifty-eight of sixty-three hours.

l: hospital at Royaumont, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The hospital at Royaumont was established and operating under the French Red Cross by the end of 1914. Despite early shortages, it was equipped with beds, lighting, kitchen facilities, lavatories, and theatre sinks, and contained four wards named for Blanche of Castille, Queen Margaret of Scotland, Joan of Arc, and Millicent Fawcett.

l: medical care for the Jugoslavs, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Medical care for the Jugoslavs was provided by Elsie Inglis and her Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit on the Eastern front. They shared the Jugoslavs’ privations and misfortunes and made every effort to support them when Russian equipment and medical resources were inadequate.

l: nationality and internationalism, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: has_relationship Southern Slav unity [nationality as a foundation for internationalism] Nationality and internationalism were connected in Seton-Watson’s account of Inglis’s work. He presented nationality as a necessary foundation for a new and saner internationalism, with great and small nations alike entitled to national independence.

l: Dr. Eleanor Soltau, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Dr. Eleanor Soltau was a doctor leading the Scottish Women’s Hospitals for Foreign Service’s first unit at Kragujevatz. She commanded the First Serbian Unit during the devastating typhus epidemic, until diphtheria made her ill in spring 1915.

l: Foreign Office, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Foreign Office was responsible for the safety of Scottish Women’s Hospitals’ British outpost hospitals. It cooperated with Dr. Elsie Inglis to equip and convey units overseas, agreed stipulations that did not hinder her work, and undertook extensive care and diplomatic work for the hospitals.

l: Austro-German forces, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Austro-German forces overran Serbia in 1915, controlled areas containing Scottish medical units and Serbian hospitals, then guarded a Scottish unit sent north toward Austria.

l: the typhus epidemic, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The typhus epidemic was an epidemic in Serbia during the First World War. Beginning in filthy, overcrowded hospitals after the Austrian invasion, it swept across Serbia in spring 1915 and raged for three months, devastating Serbian people. It killed 125 of Serbia’s 425 doctors and affected two-thirds of the remainder. It made crowded-hospital work dangerous and harsh for the Scottish women. After the fever died out, the Scottish unit feared its return, but cleaning, sanitation, laundry, bathing, and education about dirt prevented cases in its hospital.

l: Mladenovatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Mladenovatz is the place where the Serbian nation built a fountain near the camp hospital to commemorate Dr. Elsie Inglis and the Scottish Women’s Hospitals. It was formally opened on 7 October 1915 with a Greek Church religious service, and later recalled as a simple fountain dedicated two years earlier.

l: simple fountain (in Mladenovatz), Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: A simple fountain in Mladenovatz, built by the Serbs in grateful memory of the Scottish Women’s Hospitals’ work. It commemorates that work and was dedicated to the memory of a woman called “the angel of their people.” At its opening, Dr. Elsie Inglis turned on the water after a Greek Church religious service, intended to flow in remembrance.

l: Dr. Inglis's funeral and burial, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Dr. Elsie Inglis’s funeral and burial took place in Edinburgh on November 29, 1917. Family, colleagues, societies, hospital officials, military personnel, Serbian representatives, and a massed crowd attended. Her Allied-flag-covered coffin travelled on a gun carriage through the city, with military honours, the Hallelujah Chorus, and Reveille, before Serbian representatives carried it to the grave.

l: women’s courage and service in wartime, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_presented_as a power to turn war’s curse to blessing [through faith in womanhood] The Scottish women faced epidemics, famine, danger, and severe privations without faltering in courage or endurance. Their service was presented as evidence of the power of womanhood to turn war’s curse toward blessing and to answer hatred with love.

l: dedication of the fountain in Mladenovatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a dedication The dedication took place two years ago and honored the grateful memory of a woman whom the Serbians called "the angel of their people."

l: Russian refugees in the Dobrudja, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Russian refugees in Dobrudja remember and will never forget the woman known as “the angel of their people.”

l: Kragujevatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Kragujevatz housed the Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit in a girls’ school and included surgical, typhus, and general-disease hospitals. The first unit under Dr. Soltau also did excellent work there after the Serbian victories in 1914.

l: Danube, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_frozen across its entire width [in the winter of 1917] The Danube freezes completely near Reni, reportedly for the first time in seven years. Cossack soldiers cross it to cut wood for the hospital.

l: the Serbian retreat of 1915, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Serbian retreat of 1915 began when German forces appeared on the northern frontier, Bulgaria invaded from the east, and Austria advanced from the west, trapping the Serbian army. Though 160,000 soldiers escaped, the retreat produced many wounded, treated at Galatz by the Scottish Women’s Hospitals working continuously.

l: the German and Bulgarian invasion of Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The German and Bulgarian invasion of Serbia was part of a wider autumn 1915 attack. Germans massed in the north, Bulgarians invaded from the east, and Austrian forces joined from the west, overwhelming Serbian defenses. The Austro-German invasion caused military collapse, refugees’ flight, soldiers’ capture, hospital abandonment or occupation, and evacuation or retreat decisions for Scottish units.

l: the typhus disease, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a infectious disease Typhus disease spread through Serbia after the Austrian invasion and caused extensive deaths among Serbian doctors and medical staff. The Scottish Women’s Hospitals treated it in infectious-disease hospitals and established or planned disinfecting work to control it.

l: the work of women in wartime, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: supports Serbian agriculture [throughout the wars] The women working in the Scottish units continued through the typhus epidemic, with none asking to leave; three died and nine became ill in one unit. Serbian women also kept the country’s agriculture going through four wars in three years, and Serbia planned a special medal to honour them.

l: Serbian wounded, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Serbian wounded, housed in great numbers at the Serbian military hospital at Krushieevatz, fill overcrowded hospitals during retreat and occupation; Scottish women tend them despite shortages.

l: Sir Ralph Paget, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: permits evacuation of the hospital units [while allowing volunteers to remain] Sir Ralph Paget considered the evacuation of the British unit and, after recognising that its equipment could not be saved, allowed members to choose whether to leave or remain with their wounded. He eventually agreed that the unit should stand by its hospitals.

l: Krushieevatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Krushieevatz, site of a Serbian military hospital, held 900 wounded in November 1915 and later 1,200 patients; during Austro-German occupation, the Scottish unit remained amid cold, hunger, refugees, prisoners, and military collapse.

l: Salonika, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Salonika was the destination where some equipment was believed to be safe and where a distant force of 150,000 British troops was expected. The unit doubted that this prospect would quickly relieve the famine and cold in the remaining Serbian territory.

l: evacuation of the hospital units, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: includes retreat via Montenegro [as one possible route] Evacuation was considered during the invasion, with one possible route through Montenegro. Two parties retreated with the Serbs, while the unit at Krushieevatz stayed after its members were offered the choice of leaving or remaining; later, the remaining unit was transported under guard.

l: captivity of the Scottish unit, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Scottish unit spent about five months under foreign occupation caring for Serbian wounded; as fever subsided, it was sent north under Austrian guard through Vienna, ending in Zürich.

l: Serbian military hospital at Krushieevatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Serbian military hospital at Krushieevatz, designed for 400 beds, held about 900 wounded on the Scottish unit’s arrival and later 1,200. As fever subsided, the unit took over sanitation and laundry and converted corridors, outhouses, a magazine, and other spaces for treatment.

l: the Zoo, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Zoo was an overcrowded hospital magazine where wounded patients occupied three tiers of shelving; as fever died out, a worse enemy arrived, and patients later filled makeshift spaces amid dim light and beans.

l: famine in Serbia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: affects Serbia [during enemy occupation] Famine threatened the parts of Serbia left outside enemy control, alongside cold and displacement. The unit observed starving civilians, weakened workers, underfed prisoners, and exhausted oxen, while its own limited supplies could not feed all the hungry people around the hospital.

l: sanitation, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_administered_by Scottish hospital unit [at the Serbian military hospital] The unit undertook sanitation work despite having no specialist, burying rubbish, emptying an overflowing cesspool, building incinerators, and repeatedly cleaning the hospital compound. It also established laundry and bathing arrangements, helping prevent typhus under severely overcrowded conditions.

l: Serbian prisoners, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Serbian prisoners, held in the military hospital at Krushieevatz after forced marches, suffer cold, hunger, scant rations, inadequate shelter, and lice; arrivals grow to thousands daily, with many sent north while the sick remain in crowded wards.

l: the S.W.H. Committees, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The S.W.H. Committees were strong, organized committees of women from Britain managing Scottish Women’s Hospitals. While Dr. Inglis served abroad, they carried the main burden of finance and administration: selecting personnel, supervising immense equipment and motor-transport shipments, dealing with the British Government, supporting Kossovo Day, and receiving reports from the Serbian mission.

l: Kossovo Day, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Kossovo Day was a successful Serbian patriotic flag-day in Great Britain, organized under Dr. Inglis’s chairmanship within six weeks. It unfolded through hundreds of lectures on Serbian history across the country and concluded as a reported success.

l: Serbian Volunteers, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Serbian Volunteers were intended to be served by the final Scottish Women’s Hospitals unit on the Rumanian Russian front.

l: Russian Revolution, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Russian Revolution is a political upheaval in Russia associated with changes reported from Petrograd and a major reverberation that altered the tone of Russian soldiers. Russian officers and patients supported the change, though revolutionary conditions fostered suspicion during a spy incident. The upheaval imperilled the Serbian Army on the Rumanian front, cut communications with Dr. Inglis’s unit, and led Inglis to send members home with verbal messages while the London Committee awaited news and urged her return.

l: Archangel, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Archangel is a Russian port city whose population grew during the war. In 1917 it was the unit’s entry point into Russia, where British naval personnel and local officials organized transport, supplies, hospitality, and a ceremonial departure onward; Elsie Maud Inglis passed through returning home.

l: Galatz, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Galatz is the fallback place for the hospitals. After equipment is recovered from a refugee train, it is brought safely there. The unit operates a hospital in a school, works through the night, later connects with Reni, and sends a messenger to fetch General Kropensky during a spy incident.

l: Newcastle, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Newcastle was the port where the transport arrived after its dangerous voyage west. Dr. Inglis left the boat there on November 25, 1917, and died shortly afterward at the Station Hotel.

l: the journey from Archangel to Odessa, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a adventurous undertaking [from Archangel through Russia to Odessa and the Dobrudja] The Russian journey took the unit from Archangel toward Moscow by special train after a rapid passage through Archangel. The travelers experienced delays, repaired couplings and engines, received food and other assistance from Russian authorities, and were welcomed by Russian soldiers and civilians.

l: the captured transport ship, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Transport carries Serbian soldiers, Dr. Inglis, her unit, and representatives toward England, faces North Sea dangers, while ill Dr. Inglis rests, treats a naval officer, reviews accounts, and plans future work.

l: the unit (British medical unit), Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: A British medical unit composed of British women, also described as Scottish Sisters in Russian service, traveled from Archangel through Moscow and Odessa to serve the Serbian 1st Division. Funded through the Russian Red Cross, it ran two field hospitals, at Medgidia and near the front at Bulbulmic, and later worked at Braila, Galatz, and Reni. During retreat it evacuated people and equipment, then treated Serbian, Rumanian, and Russian wounded amid cold, mud, shortages, overcrowding, suspicion, and language difficulties. Members received St. George Medals.

l: the Serbian medical units, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a medical units [serving Serbian patients] The Serbian medical units included two small field hospitals assigned to serve a whole division. Elsie sought to establish a Serbian hospital and tried to coordinate with Serbian Hospital H. 2, while Serbian wounded were generally evacuated directly to Odessa.

l: Russian soldiers, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Russian soldiers, treated as patients at the Scottish Women’s Hospital at Reni, thank Elsie and her unit for their care and attention. They receive cigarettes and Easter eggs, attend religious services, and support the unit during a spy incident. They publicly defend the hospital’s supplies and tell the local Commandant it is the best hospital on the front.

l: Russians, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Russians are the unit’s official and local hosts, supporters, patients, and allies. They provide base hospitals for Serbian wounded and their own troops; near Odessa, officials, hospitals, soldiers, and officers assist the unit, while Russian wounded form most of its patients. Soldiers and citizens express gratitude and hope in the Allied cause, welcome changes in Petrograd, and support the hospital. The records end by calling them, especially common soldiers, fascinating people treated by the English Sisters.

l: Medgidia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: contains the hospital at Medgidia [in a barrack building] Medgidia was the site of the unit’s main hospital, housed in a barrack, with personnel living in tents on the opposite hill. The unit arrived during the offensive, made the hospital operational within forty-eight hours, and remained there for less than three weeks before retreating.

l: Braila, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: receives the shortage of medical staff [during the influx of wounded] Braila received an enormous influx of wounded during the retreat, with approximately 7,000 to 11,000 patients and only seven doctors, one of them a surgeon. The unit went there to help, found wounded lying in houses and without dressed wounds for several days, and worked until the immediate pressure had passed.

l: Petrograd, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_site_of Russian Revolution [news received by the unit] News from Petrograd causes excitement among Elsie and her unit. Russian officers and patients generally support the change and describe it as a significant political development.

l: the retreat from Medgidia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: A military retreat marked by panic and displacement: a field hospital, transport, and personnel withdrew as refugees and disorganized Russian, Serbian, and Rumanian soldiers crowded roads, abandoning equipment en route through Caramacat and Hershova to Braila.

l: the evacuation of Medgidia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a wartime hospital evacuation [conducted during the retreat] The evacuation of Medgidia required the unit to dismantle and move its hospital equipment while continuing to nurse, operate, and evacuate patients. The transport and personnel were sent away in stages, and the unit ultimately lost two cars, one Ludgate boiler, and one box of radiators.

l: the hospital at Medgidia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a main hospital [of the British medical unit] The hospital at Medgidia was established in a barrack and made ready for patients within forty-eight hours of the unit’s arrival. The unit unpacked and repacked its equipment there, operated and nursed patients, and evacuated the hospital during the retreat.

l: the field hospital at Bulbulmic, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a field hospital [about seven miles from the front] The field hospital at Bulbulmic was about seven miles from the front. It was brought back five versts at the beginning of the retreat, after which its transport and personnel were moved onward.

l: the ambulance train, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie writes from an ambulance train near Odessa after the unit has worked in hospitals for Serbian, Rumanian, and Russian patients. The train's movement brings the unit close to the front, where it narrowly leaves before a station is burned.

l: the shortage of medical staff, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The shortage of medical staff was a critical wartime hospital deficiency at Braila: 11,000 wounded were initially reported, but only seven doctors, including one surgeon, served two small field hospitals, prompting a request for another base hospital.

l: Scottish Women's Hospital at Reni, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Scottish Women's Hospital at Reni is a hospital run by the unit and operated by Scottish Women's Hospitals. It treats Russian and Serbian soldiers, sailors, and other wounded patients, with icons for Russian religious use, tents for personnel, and care inspected for cleanliness, food, nursing, and medicine. Russian soldiers regard it as the best hospital on the front and defend its needs. It continues work through mud, weather, fuel shortages, and a spy investigation.

l: Easter, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_celebrated_by the unit [with services, eggs, and cigarettes] At Easter, Russian patients and soldiers thank Elsie and her unit for their care and express hope in the Allied cause. The unit attends or holds services, sings Easter hymns, exchanges Russian greetings, and gives patients Easter eggs and cigarettes.

l: refugees, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: travel_with carts [carrying salvaged possessions and children] Refugees in the Dobrudja travel in crowded carts carrying salvaged furniture, pots, pans, pigs, and children. Elsie describes villages along their route as deserted.

l: spy incident, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: A spy incident in which a foreign hospital near the front is suspected amid spy fever and revolutionary unrest; General Kropensky intervenes, the unit is cleared and apologized to, and its conduct preserves Russian confidence in England.

l: Mrs. Flinders Petrie, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Mrs. Flinders Petrie, Hon. Secretary, supports Scottish Women’s Hospitals through home fundraising and administration, encouraging subscriptions and receiving Inglis’s requests to hasten relief personnel.

l: hospital closure and transfer to the Serbian Division, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Reni hospital closes in late August 1917 after eight months, transferring personnel to the Serbian Division after treating mostly Russian patients and emergencies.

l: Russian and Serbian military medical work, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: is_a wartime hospital work [performed by Scottish Women's Hospitals] The unit provides medical care to Russian and Serbian soldiers, performs prolonged operations, manages shortages of equipment and relief personnel, and works alongside military formations. Its medical work continues at Reni before transferring with the Serbian Division.

l: the Serbian evacuation from Russia, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: The Serbian evacuation from Russia, Dr. Elsie Inglis’s final central task, unfolded through wires, planning, organization, and travel with Serbian soldiers and her unit west to England.

l: Dr. Inglis's death, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: occurs_in Newcastle [after the voyage west] Dr. Inglis's death followed a prolonged illness, severe weakness, and a relapse during the voyage west. In Newcastle she spoke calmly of going to the other side, sent messages to those she remembered, heard words about the life beyond, and died peacefully.

l: the voyage west, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: uses the transport [to bring the unit home] The voyage west carried Dr. Inglis, her unit, the H.G. Staff, and Serbian soldiers from Russia toward England. It included fifteen days on a train, a difficult embarkation at Archangel, a dangerous sea passage, and the near collision and breaking of the transport's moorings before arrival at Newcastle.

l: the equipment, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: includes medical supplies [needed by the hospitals] The equipment was Dr. Inglis's constant concern during bombardments, retreats, and evacuations. Members of the unit recovered trucks carrying it after they went onto the wrong line, and ingenuity was used to bring it safely through to Galatz.

l: the moorings, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: break the transport [during a storm on the Tyne] The moorings of the transport broke during a storm after a large liner came within a foot of cutting the vessel in two. Dr. Inglis interpreted this event as an image of her own approaching death, saying that the same hand that had cut her moorings was cutting hers.

l: Red Cross service, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: Elsie Inglis was honored as a worker and leader of the Red Cross whose service had aided Serbia and other people affected by the war. Her funeral included military honors for what was described as the service of a happy warrior of the Red Cross.

l: Dr. Inglis's last message, Dr. Elsie Inglis
s: A November 26, 1917 message, dictated through Evelyn Simson to the London Committee for S.W.H., apologizes for inability to go to London, asks hospitality for Serbian representatives, and urges support for Serbia through hospitals and transport, while thanking the committee.

Not in a frantic rushing about from place to place, glancing at everything and observing nothing; flying from town to town, from hotel to hotel, eager to "do" and to see a country, in order that when they get home they may say they have done it, and seen it. Only to say;--as for any real vision of eye, heart, and brain, they might as well go through the world blindfold. It is not the things we see, but the mind we see them with, which makes the real interest of travelling. "Eyes and No Eyes,"--an old-fashioned story about two little children taking a walk; one seeing everything, and enjoying everything, and the other seeing nothing, and thinking the expedition the dullest imaginable. This simple tale, which the present generation has probably never read, contains the essence of all rational travelling. So when, as the "old hen," (which I am sometimes called, from my habit of going about with a brood of "chickens," my own or other people's) I planned a brief tour with two of

s: make ourselves happy in our own humble, feminine way. Not 'roughing it' in any needless or reckless fashion--the 'old hen' is too old for that; yet doing everything with reasonable economy. Above all, rushing into no foolhardy exploits, and taking every precaution to keep well and strong, so as to enjoy the journey from beginning to end, and hinder no one else from enjoying it. There are four things which travellers ought never to lose: their luggage, their temper, their health, and their spirits. I will make you as happy as I possibly can, but you must also make me happy by following my rules: especially the one golden rule, Obey orders." So preached the "old hen," with a vague fear that her chickens might turn out to be ducklings, which would be a little awkward in the region whither she proposed to take them. For if there is one place more risky than another for adventurous young people with a talent for "perpetuating themselves down prejudices," as Mrs. Malaprop would say, it is that grandest, wildest, most dangerous coast, the coast of Cornwall. I had always wished to investigate Cornwall. This desire had existed ever since, at five years old, I made acquaintance

s: most dangerous coast, the coast of Cornwall. I had always wished to investigate Cornwall. This desire had existed ever since, at five years old, I made acquaintance with Jack the Giantkiller, and afterwards, at fifteen or so, fell in love with my life's one hero, King Arthur. Between these two illustrious Cornishmen,--equally mythical, practical folk would say--there exists more similarity than at first appears. The aim of both was to uphold right and to redress wrong. Patience, self-denial; tenderness to the weak and helpless, dauntless courage against the wicked and the strong: these, the essential elements of true manliness, characterise both the humble Jack and the kingly Arthur. And the qualities seem to have descended to more modern times. The well-known ballad:-- "And shall they scorn Tre, Pol, and Pen? And shall Trelawny die? The climate, Charles told me, is so mild, that invalids often settle down in the one inn--a mere village inn externally, but very comfortable. And, as I afterwards heard at Lizard Town, the parson and his wife--"didn't I know them?" and I felt myself rather looked down upon because I did not know them--are the kindest of people, who take pleasure in looking after the invalids, rich or poor.
